body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Remote monitoring after cardiac surgery and 30-day readmission: a randomised trial","authors":"Lindberg-Asante K, Moreau-Obi T, Castellanos-Pryor J","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Cardiothoracic Recovery","doi":"10.5555/jcr.2022.0371","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomly allocated 610 adults discharged after cardiac surgery to 30 days of remote monitoring with daily nurse review of blood pressure, weight, rhythm and symptoms, or to usual follow-up. Thirty-day readmission was 9.2 percent with remote monitoring and 12.8 percent with usual care (risk ratio 0.72, 95 percent CI 0.47 to 1.10). Emergency department visits without admission were 11 percent and 17 percent. Atrial fibrillation was detected earlier with monitoring. Patients reported high satisfaction, and 8 percent stopped transmitting before day 30. The trial was not powered for readmission and did not collect costs."},{"title":"Cost-effectiveness of remote monitoring after cardiac surgery: a model-based analysis","authors":"Achterberg-Singh D, Nwosu-Hallam E","year":2023,"venue":"Cardiovascular Health Economics","providerType":"economic evaluation","abstract":"We built a decision model with a 90-day horizon and a health system perspective, taking the effect on readmission from a single randomised trial. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was 18,500 per quality-adjusted life year. In probabilistic analysis, remote monitoring had a 54 percent probability of being cost-effective at a threshold of 50,000 per quality-adjusted life year. Results were driven almost entirely by the readmission effect, whose confidence interval crossed no effect. The authors recommend a real-world comparison across hospitals to estimate the effect before funding decisions."},{"title":"Variation in readmission after cardiac surgery across hospitals: the role of case mix and discharge practices","authors":"Okonjo-Brandt P, Silva-Nakamura H, Reid-Adeyemi F","year":2020,"venue":"Surgical Outcomes Research","doi":"10.5555/sor.2020.0188","providerType":"cohort study","abstract":"We studied 28,400 patients discharged after cardiac surgery from 12 hospitals over four years. Thirty-day readmission varied from 9 to 19 percent across hospitals. Case mix, including age, frailty, ejection fraction, urgency and procedure type, explained about half of the variation between hospitals. Hospitals with early follow-up calls had lower adjusted readmission, but the association was confounded by hospital volume. The authors warn that comparisons of programmes between hospitals must adjust for case mix and account for stable differences between hospitals."},{"title":"Remote patient monitoring after surgery: a systematic review of readmission and emergency department visits","authors":"Haugen-Mbeki A, Olsen-Carvalho R, Tan-Whitaker M","year":2024,"venue":"Perioperative Care Reviews","doi":"10.5555/pcr.2024.0066","providerType":"systematic review","abstract":"We included 21 studies of remote patient monitoring after surgery, 7 of them randomised. Across all studies, readmission was lower with monitoring (risk ratio 0.81, 95 percent CI 0.68 to 0.97), but the effect was smaller in randomised studies. In the cardiac surgery subgroup of 6 studies, the risk ratio was 0.84 (95 percent CI 0.64 to 1.10). Emergency department visits were reduced in most studies. Few studies reported costs, and none compared hospitals that adopted monitoring with hospitals that did not while accounting for trends before adoption."},{"title":"Patients' and carers' experience of home monitoring after heart surgery: an interview study","authors":"Farrow-Ekwueme L, Johansson-Diaz C","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Cardiac Nursing Experience","doi":"10.5555/jcne.2021.0240","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 20 patients and 12 carers after 30 days of home monitoring following cardiac surgery. Most described reassurance from knowing a nurse was reviewing their readings. Some found alerts about minor changes worrying and phoned the hospital more as a result. Older patients often depended on a carer to set up and use the devices. Several patients in rural areas lost connection for days. Participants wanted to know in advance what would happen when an alert fired, and carers asked for a named contact at the hospital."},{"title":"Comparing adopting and non-adopting hospitals in health services evaluation: difference-in-differences with few sites","authors":"Varga-Holloway S, Kim-Ogunleye B","year":2019,"venue":"Health Services Methods","doi":"10.5555/hsm.2019.0031","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examine methods for estimating programme effects when a few hospitals adopt a programme and others do not. Differences between hospitals that are stable over time can be removed by comparing changes before and after adoption, but only if outcomes followed parallel trends before adoption. With only two adopting and two comparison hospitals, conventional standard errors are far too small; a wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference gives honest intervals. Contamination, when a comparison hospital adopts part of the programme, biases the estimate towards no effect and should be handled by ending the comparison period at the contamination date."},{"title":"Health system costs in the 90 days after discharge from cardiac surgery","authors":"Provincial Costing Unit Analysts","year":2025,"venue":"Provincial Health Costing Reports","providerType":"report","abstract":"We priced all health system contacts in the 90 days after discharge for 9,800 cardiac surgery patients using provincial case costing. The mean cost after discharge was 6,200 per patient. Readmissions accounted for 58 percent of this cost, emergency department visits for 9 percent and physician visits for 14 percent. Costs were highest for patients readmitted with infection or heart failure. Costs of home care and medications were not included because they are not held in the provincial data, so total costs are understated."}]}
